tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the independent lzbench 2.4 suite (public code, inikep/lzbench; gcc 15.2.0 release binary; single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P, turbo off, silesia.tar) lists memlz 0.5 beta at 4452 MB/s compress, 2039 MB/s decompress, 59.90% vs lz4 1.10.0 --fast -17 at 924 / 3977 MB/s, 62.15% and snappy 1.3.1 at 457 / 976 MB/s, 47.85%. Compile flags are not on the results page, so B, not A (consistent with lzav, lzsse, misa77 in this wave).

corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (silesia.tar, one thread of an EPYC 9555P): memlz 0.5 beta compresses at 4452 MB/s and decompresses at 2039 MB/s at 59.90% size, vs lz4 1.10.0 at 550 / 3832 MB/s, 47.60%; lz4 --fast -17 at 924 / 3977 MB/s, 62.15%; snappy 1.3.1 at 457 / 976 MB/s, 47.85%; lzo1x 2.10 -1 at 500 / 561 MB/s; fastlz 0.5.0 -1 at 273 / 587 MB/s; memcpy 24075 MB/s. Compression is about 4.8x lz4 --fast -17, 8.1x default lz4 and 9.7x snappy (derived from page data); decompression is about 0.53x lz4 (slower) and 2.1x snappy (derived from page data). First-party README: '5 - 7 GB/s in one thread'; its Figure_1.png (Intel i7, model not stated) plots memlz compression at roughly 5800 MB/s on Silesia vs roughly 2250 MB/s for LZ4-64 (approximate, read from graph).
corrections.hardware: Independent: single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off (lzbench 2.4). First-party README figures: Intel i7 (model not stated) with 14000 MB/s non-cached memcpy.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, run with -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; per-codec flags are not on the results page (inikep/lzbench Makefile default is -O3 -DNDEBUG -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing)
corrections.workload: Single-thread in-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar in lzbench 2.4 (independent); first-party README figures cover enwik8, Silesia and employees_50MB.json.
corrections.caveats: Compression-speed win only: decompression is about half of LZ4's speed in lzbench and the ratio (59.90%) is much worse than lz4 default or snappy (about 47.6-47.9%); the fair comparison is lz4 --fast -17 (62.15%, 924 MB/s). lzbench measured 4452 MB/s, below the README's 5-7 GB/s claim (different CPU). Beta format, compatibility may break. lzbench patches memlz.h for MinGW (SSE4.2 target attribute).

notes: README numbers live in PNG figures (opened them: Figure_1 compress, Figure_2 decompress, LZ4/zstd-1/blosclz/Chameleon only); the stronger evidence is the lzbench table, which lists memlz alongside lz4, snappy, lzo, fastlz. Metadata OK: MIT, 79 stars, last commit 2026-10-02.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: zlib-ng/pigzbench is an independent third-party harness (public Python scripts a_compile.py, b_speed_threads.py, c_decompress.py, d_speed_size.py; not by the pigz author) on a named CPU (12-core AMD Ryzen 3900X) that compares pigz with system zlib against gzip; compiler and flags are not stated (CMake defaults in a_compile.py), so not A. It is a small repo (17 stars), so the 'independent measurement' reading of B is the generous one; C is defensible if B requires a well-known suite.

corrections.claimed_speedup: pigzbench README table, decompression speed (MB/s): pigz-Sys 306, pigz-CF 307, pigz-ng 361, gzip 189, pbzip2 448, zstd 528; pigz with system zlib is about 1.6x gzip (derived from page data). Compression appears only in graphs (approximate, read from silesia_speed_threads.png and silesia_speed_size.png): at 1 thread pigz with system zlib plots at about the same speed as gzip at each level; at 12 threads pigz-System level 3 reaches roughly 490 MB/s vs gzip level 3 at roughly 65 MB/s, and README text says 'All versions of pigz outperform the system's single threaded gzip'.
corrections.hardware: 12-core (24-thread) AMD Ryzen 3900X for the thread-scaling graph; the README does not say which machine produced the decompression table.
corrections.compiler_and_flags: Not stated; a_compile.py builds pigz against madler/zlib, cloudflare/zlib and zlib-ng (develop, -DZLIB_COMPAT=ON) with CMake defaults.
corrections.caveats: No own-code single-thread compression win: the compression gain over gzip comes from multithreading (at 1 thread pigz-System and gzip plot together), and the larger gains in the table come from the zlib backend (zlib-ng, Cloudflare), which the catalog lists separately. Decompression gain over gzip (306 vs 189 MB/s with the same system zlib) is real but comes from pigz's zlib inflate plus separate read/write/check threads, not a new algorithm. Compiler and flags not stated; compression numbers only in graphs. Maintenance 'abandoned' by the 3-year rule (last commit 2023-08-20, v2.8). pigzbench is a port of neurolabusc/pigz-bench-python (its graph links point there).

notes: Per catalog rule: pigz judged on pigzbench; it carries a multithreading win only for compression (no own-code single-thread win) and a modest pipelining win for decompression; zlib-ng/libdeflate wins belong to those entries. Metadata OK: zlib license (SPDX Zlib), 3.0k stars, not archived, last commit 2023-08-20.

tier_reason: Upgraded from C: the independent lzbench 2.4 suite (public code, gcc 15.2.0 release binary, single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P, silesia.tar) lists snappy 1.3.1 at 457 / 976 MB/s, 47.85% vs zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 / 297 MB/s, 36.45%. Flags are not on the results page, so B, not A. The README's own Core i7 numbers remain first-party.

corrections.claimed_speedup: lzbench 2.4 (silesia.tar, one thread of an EPYC 9555P): snappy 1.3.1 compresses at 457 MB/s and decompresses at 976 MB/s at 47.85% size vs zlib 1.3.2 -1 at 89.0 / 297 MB/s, 36.45%: about 5.1x faster compression and 3.3x faster decompression than zlib's fastest level, with output about 31% larger (derived from page data). Against zlib-ng 2.3.3 -1 (196 / 466 MB/s, 44.41%) the margin is about 2.3x / 2.1x (derived from page data). README (first-party, Core i7, model not stated): 'an order of magnitude faster' than zlib's fastest mode for most inputs, about 250 MB/s compress and 500 MB/s decompress or more on the slowest inputs.
corrections.hardware: Independent: single thread of an AMD EPYC 9555P at 3.20 GHz, turbo off (lzbench 2.4). README: single core of a Core i7 in 64-bit mode (model not stated).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: lzbench 2.4 release binary built with gcc 15.2.0, run with -eALL -t8,8 -o1c4; per-codec flags are not on the results page (inikep/lzbench Makefile default is -O3 -DNDEBUG -fomit-frame-pointer -fstrict-aliasing)
corrections.workload: Single-thread in-memory compression and decompression of silesia.tar in lzbench 2.4; the README's numbers come from Snappy's own testdata suite.
corrections.caveats: The independent measurement shows about 5x (compress) and 3x (decompress) over zlib -1, not the README's 'order of magnitude'. Modern codecs beat it in the same table: lz4 1.10.0 at 550 / 3832 MB/s with a similar ratio (47.60%), and zstd 1.5.7 -1 at 411 / 1351 MB/s with a much better ratio (34.53%). README numbers are first-party with no CPU model, compiler or flags.

notes: README claims verified verbatim; lzbench gives the third-party numbers. Metadata OK: BSD-3-Clause, 6.6k stars, last commit 2026-09-18 (v1.3.1).
